title: "No way to prevent this" say users of only language where this regularly happens
content: In the hours following the release of CVE-2026-94300 for the project BIND 9 named, site reliability workers and systems administrators scrambled to desperately rebuild and patch all their systems to fix memory corruption in named triggered by replaying captured GSS-TSIG-signed UDP messages while the negotiated TSIG key remains valid, potentially allowing remote code execution when combined with crafted queries to an attacker-controlled zone. This is due to the affected components being written in C, the only programming language where these vulnerabilities regularly happen. "This was a terrible tragedy, but sometimes these things just happen and there's nothing anyone can do to stop them," said programmer Queen Aniya Rippin, echoing statements expressed by hundreds of thousands of programmers who use the only language where 90% of the world's memory safety vulnerabilities have occurred in the last 50 years, and whose projects are 20 times more likely to have security vulnerabilities. "It's a shame, but what can we do? There really isn't anything we can do to prevent memory safety vulnerabilities from happening if the programmer doesn't want to write their code in a robust manner." At press time, users of the only programming language in the world where these vulnerabilities regularly happen once or twice per quarter for the last eight years were referring to themselves and their situation as "helpless."

title: Why didn’t we use Ro­Register­For­Apartment­Shutdown to clean up the unmarshalable delegate?
content:
In my attempt to create a fake agile wrapper that is technically agile but is not useful outside its home apartment, Luca Bacci suggested, among other things, using the Ro­Register­For­Apartment­Shutdown function.

The Ro­Register­For­Apartment­Shutdown function is nice, but it doesn’t suit our needs.

One problem is that the object registered for apartment shutdown must be agile. (If you pass a non-agile object, the call fails.) That means that our wrapper must be agile. If we put the non-marshalable non-agile object inside our wrapper, we now have an agile object (the wrapper) that holds a non-agile object (the original object) as a member, which creates the risk that the wrapper will run down in the wrong apartment. The normal way of fixing that is to use Ro­Get­Agile­Reference to create an agile wrapper around the non-agile object, and store that agile wrapper in our container object.

This puts us back where we started: We are trying to implement that agile wrapper!

Even if we got past that problem, we have another problem: At apartment shutdown, COM calls the wrapper object’s UnInitialize method, and there’s a warning on the using the Ro­Unregister­For­Apartment­Shutdown function:

Warning: Don’t call the Ro­Unregister­For­Apartment­Shutdown function from the OnUninitialize callback.

But wait, what if the destructor of the object we are wrapping wants to call Ro­Unregister­For­Apartment­Shutdown? It might happen indirectly because it has its own reference to another object, that in turn tries to call Ro­Unregister­For­Apartment­Shutdown.

For example, it might hold another fake agile wrapper whose UnInitialize method has already been called! (We can work around that in our agile wrapper by nulling out the non-agile pointer so we don’t double-release, but maybe there’s some other object that uses Ro­Unregister­For­Apartment­Shutdown that is less resilient to this scenario.)

Another requirement of Ro­Unregister­For­Apartment­Shutdown is that it must be called from the same apartment that registered. This doesn’t quite put us back where we started, but it makes things more complicated because the whole point of the exercise is to find a way to release the object without having to try to switch to the apartment. I guess what we could do is use IContext­Callback to try to switch back to the apartment to release the original object and unregister the apartment shutdown callback. If the apartment switch fails, then we assume it’s because the apartment has already run down, so we assume that the IApartment­Shutdown::On­Uninitialize method was called, and it released the object for us. (Of course, that still creates the problem that we are cleaning up inside the On­Uninitialize callback, which meas that nobody else can unregister their apartment shutdown callback.)

The last note on this is that the implementation is written on the assumption that there are not a lot of apartment shutdown callbacks. Registration is O(1), but unregistration is O(n) because it does a linear search through all of the apartment’s registered shutdown callbacks to find the one being unregistered. By comparison, the Global Interface Table is designed on the assumption that it will have to manage a lot of objects, so it can look up its cookies in O(1) time. The proposed alternate design would register and unregister a lot of apartment shutdown callbacks, so it’s pushing the apartment shutdown callback list into a usage pattern it wasn’t optimized for.

title: Backdoors, Incompetence, and Elliptic Curves
content:
The NIST elliptic curves have been in the news twice lately. A few days ago Anthropic posted a paper on the NIST curve seeds that I wrote about here. Now the curves are in the news again, this time over broken certificates.

My post a few days ago was about the possibility that the NSA had added a backdoor to the NIST curves. Anthropic researchers showed that this wasn’t the case. The NSA had not been able to defend how the curve seeds were chosen because they forgot, but researchers from Anthropic were able to reverse engineer the source of the seeds.

So apparently the NIST curves do not have a backdoor, but as with all encryption, the Achilles heel is human error. eMudrha was using the NIST curve P-384  with extremely small keys: 4, 56, 115, 155, 156, 230, and 237. To understand why this is a problem, I’ll briefly describe how elliptic curve cryptography works.

P-384 is an elliptic curve designed by NIST, with input from the NSA, for use in cryptography. The curve has on the order of 2384 points [1] because the base field is the integers mod

p = 2384 − 2128 − 296 + 232 − 1,

a 384-bit prime number. Given a basepoint b on the curve and an exponent e, it is practically impossible to recover e from be. That’s the discrete logarithm problem [2], the basis for the security of elliptic curve cryptography. If and when cryptographically relevant quantum computers arrive, the discrete logarithm problem will be solvable and elliptic curve cryptography will be broken.

Until the advent of quantum computing, elliptic curve cryptography is presumably safe, unless someone does something negligent, such as using a tiny value of e like 4.

If e is chosen at random from a group with on the order of 2384 elements, you cannot recover e from be without brute force. But apparently someone said

Let’s see. Is e = 1? Is it 2? Is it 3? Is it 4? Why yes: e = 4.

Ordinarily this would be hopeless. You can’t just try 2384 exponents. But someone thought to test whether the keys were horrifically bad, and they were right.

 

[1] I don’t know whether the exact number of points on the curve is known. It’s the number of points on an elliptic curve is not simple to calculate, but it is easy to estimate. It’s roughly the size of the base field, which is p.

Update: There are exactly 39402006196394479212279040100143613805079739270465446667946905279627659399113263569398956308152294913554433653942643 points on the P384 curve. (NIST SP 800-186, §3.2.1.4⁠)

[2] The exponentiation here is not over the integers, or over the integers mod p. It’s over the group structure of the elliptic curve, and that is what makes it hard to compute the discrete logarithm.

title: Trust Stores Are Dependencies Too
content:
eMudhra generated eight of its intermediate CA certificates incorrectly, so their private keys can be recovered from the certificates themselves. Firefox (OneCRL and CRLite) and Chrome (CRLSets) blocked the intermediates on 17 October, Apple on the 19th, and Microsoft on the 20th through Windows’ automatic trust list updates. The disclosure page states that “many other clients do not consume revocation information and require software updates”, and its fix table lists the packages that carry their own copy of the roots:

  • certifi 2026.10.19 and pip 26.2.2
  • uv 0.13.4 and pixi 0.82.1
  • webpki-roots and webpki-root-certs 1.0.10, rustls-webpki 0.103.16, rustup 1.29.2
  • Node.js 22.23.4, 24.22.1 and 26.12.1
  • Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10
  • Composer’s ca-bundle, Elixir’s castore 1.0.22, Perl’s Mozilla::CA 20261020
  • the curl CA bundle, NSS 3.131.1, and a row of Linux distributions
  • the pip3 shipped with macOS, which uses “its own outdated copy of the roots”

Michał Górny, who maintains a large part of Gentoo’s Python packaging, traced where certifi alone ends up. Gentoo’s certifi is patched to use the system store, so system Python picks up the change when ca-certificates updates. Everywhere else needs its own update:

  • Each virtualenv and conda environment that installs certifi has its own copy.
  • pip vendors certifi, so every environment’s pip needs upgrading, using the old pip to fetch the new one.
  • Python vendors pip through ensurepip to bootstrap new environments, so anywhere ensurepip installs its bundled wheel you wait for a Python release, or upgrade pip after every python -m venv.
  • Lockfiles need certifi bumped, and dependency cooldowns need an exception for it, because a cooldown on a trust store delays the fix.
  • Rust tools like uv compile webpki-roots into the binary, so each one needs a rebuild and a release, and so does any container image that includes them.
  • Flatpak runtimes each carry their own ca-certificates, and some Flatpak apps carry another copy inside that.

Bundles in critical packages

To find the routes beyond the well-known ones, I pointed git-pkgs/certs at the 6,877 packages that ecosyste.ms marks as critical across PyPI, npm, crates.io, Go, Maven Central, Packagist, NuGet and RubyGems. It downloads each package archive, reads every file statically, and pulls out anything that parses as an X.509 certificate. 116 of those packages contained certificates, about 1.7%, mostly test fixtures and package-signing certs. 28 of them ship something that works as a CA bundle. A separate RubyGems sample added a 29th, honeybadger, from outside the critical list. The full results for all 29 give each package’s version and how it loads its bundle.

The real number may be higher, because the scanner reads PEM, DER, JKS and PKCS#12 and skips certificates compiled into native code, and 49 of the 50 platform-specific Python wheels in the sample contained compiled binaries outside those formats. Across the 29, the same cacert.pem sets the trusted roots for every TLS connection in some packages and is loaded only on request, or not at all, in others:

  • Excon, pip and redshift-connector load their bundle alongside the system roots. A root removed from the OS store stays trusted, because the bundle adds it back.
  • Stripe’s Ruby library and httpclient on MRI build their own OpenSSL::X509::Store from the bundle and hand it to the connection, so a ca-certificates update leaves them trusting the same roots as before.
  • Honeybadger, aws-sdk-v1, Guzzle 3, stripe-php and braintree_php point OpenSSL or curl at their own file by default, and a configured path overrides it. gRPC’s Ruby, PHP and Python packages register their bundled roots as the default.
  • botocore and the AWS CLI use their bundled file when certifi is absent. httplib2 uses its own after checking configured paths, and two of Google’s Java clients fall back to a bundled keystore when the Java installation store is missing. Whether a given deployment hits the fallback depends on what else is installed there.
  • aws-sdk-core uses system roots by default and switches to its bundle when you call Aws.use_bundled_cert!, and gocertifi, Composer’s ca-bundle and ioredis’s RedisCloud profile likewise take effect only when code selects them. nap uses its bundled file once the caller turns on certificate verification.
  • libv8 carries a bundle inside its vendored copy of depot_tools, and App Engine’s API stubs use theirs for the local development server. virtualenv’s embedded pip wheels each contain a certifi. These ship to every install and are separate from an application’s own HTTPS requests, except that virtualenv installs its wheels as the pip in each environment it creates.

Removed roots

Matching the certificate sets against historical Mozilla releases dates honeybadger’s bundle to 2011 and httpclient’s to 2014 or 2015. Both gems are maintained: httpclient 2.9.0 came out in February 2025 and honeybadger 6.9.3 in September 2026, and both releases still ship those bundles.

Algoliasearch, aws-sdk-v1 (last released in April 2017) and Guzzle 3 (whose repository is archived) still contain StartCom roots that Mozilla removed in Firefox 58 in 2017, and those roots stay valid until 2036 and 2039. 26 of the 29 bundle packages contain at least one root that Mozilla has removed from its programme and that is still inside its validity period. Matching exact fingerprints against CCADB’s records gives 95 such roots across those packages.

eMudhra issued the compromised intermediates from its emSign Root TLS CA - G3, which emSign ECC Root CA - G3 cross-signs. Root TLS CA - G3 itself is in none of the scanned bundles, so the cross-signing root is the one that matters here. Sectigo also cross-signed each intermediate from its AAA Certificate Services root, a 2004 Comodo certificate valid until 2028. A client that uses a bundle containing emSign ECC Root CA - G3 or AAA Certificate Services as its trust anchors, and skips revocation checks, will accept a chain running from a leaf through a compromised intermediate to that root, because the attacker supplies the intermediates in the TLS handshake.

Mozilla removed emSign ECC Root CA - G3 in response to the incident, as its 20 October notice records, so it is one of the 95. The root is in ten of the packages I scanned: Excon, Stripe’s Ruby and PHP libraries, gRPC for Ruby, PHP and Python, Composer’s ca-bundle, gocertifi, App Engine’s API stubs and virtualenv. certifi carried it through 2026.7.22 and dropped it in 2026.10.18, a day before the 2026.10.19 release in the fix table, and a lockfile pinned to 2026.7.22 or another release that included it still installs it.

Mozilla ended AAA’s TLS trust in 2025, and certifi dropped it in 2025.4.26. It isn’t among the 95 above, which only counts certificates Mozilla removed from its programme outright. It’s still in 17 of the packages I scanned, including honeybadger, httpclient, aws-sdk-v1, Guzzle 3, algoliasearch, nap, gocertifi, httplib2 and botocore’s fallback. Honeybadger, httpclient on MRI, aws-sdk-v1 and Guzzle 3 use that file as the trust anchor by default, and algoliasearch adds it to an existing store, while the other twelve use it as a fallback or when code selects it.

pip 26.2.2 vendors certifi 2026.10.19, which contains neither root. botocore merged a fix removing AAA from its fallback bundle on 20 October, but the latest botocore release still ships it. AWS updated aws-sdk-core’s 2018 bundle the same day the issue was reported and Excon replaced its bundle in 1.8.0, released on 21 October, while gRPC’s backport is still open.

Package metadata

Finding all of this took downloading and parsing every file in nearly seven thousand archives, because the only record of a bundled trust store is the file itself. The manifest, lockfile and SBOM for an app using httpclient record httpclient 2.9.0, a checksum, and pkg:gem/httpclient@2.9.0. What the app depends on for TLS is Mozilla’s root list as it stood in 2014, and those documents record it only as httpclient’s name and version. When a root gets pulled, vulnerability scanners and dependency bots downstream match on those names and versions, so a search for “contains AAA Certificate Services” has to start from archive contents.

Vlad Miricioiu describes the same gap for compiled code in Binary Dependencies: Identifying the Hidden Packages We All Depend On. A Python wheel that bundles a precompiled C library depends on that library, “even though these dependency relationships are invisible to us”, because the wheel’s metadata lists only its Python dependencies. A CA bundle is what he calls a phantom binary dependency, with a PEM file in place of a .so. It’s third-party data, maintained upstream by Mozilla’s root programme on its own release schedule, copied into a package by hand at some point and then carried forward through every release after.

When an application depends on certifi directly, its lockfile names certifi and a version, and tools can track it. pip vendors certifi and records the version in src/pip/_vendor/vendor.txt, but that file is a convention of pip’s source repository, and the installed wheel’s metadata lists pip alone. webpki-roots shows up in uv’s Cargo.lock, but the uv binary you install from PyPI or Homebrew ships as a single executable with the roots compiled in and the lockfile left behind.

A file called cacert.pem inside a gem appears only in the archive’s file listing, and finding out which roots it holds means parsing it. Few registry schemas have a field for “this package vendors a copy of X at version Y”. Debian’s Built-Using field records statically linked sources, and CycloneDX’s pedigree records where a component’s contents came from. The generators that produce most SBOMs build from lockfiles, so httpclient’s entry records httpclient 2.9.0 and omits the 2014 root list inside it.
description: 26 of 29 CA bundles in critical packages contain roots Mozilla has removed.

title: No Need for Retirement When Utopia Is Around the Corner
content:
I’ve mentioned before my interest in the history and development of nuclear weapons.

Currently, I’m reading The Doomsday Machine: Confessions of a Nuclear War Planner by Daniel Ellsberg (of Pentagon Papers renown).

In the first chapter, Ellsberg talks about his time working at the RAND Corporation during the missile gap years when the U.S. thought it was falling behind the Soviet Union in nuclear capabilities.

Many of his descriptions sound strikingly similar to the rhetoric coming out of places like Anthropic. For example, note the religious overtones of working at a corporation:

I loved RAND, where I ended up spending ten years [...] Much, I imagined, like members of a religious order would, I shared with my colleagues a sense of brotherhood, living and working with others for a transcendent cause.

They were insiders: burdened with the responsibility of knowledge others did not possess.

precisely in my early missile-gap years at RAND and as a consultant in Washington, there was our sense of mission, the burden of believing we knew more about the dangers ahead, and what might be done about them, than did the generals in the Pentagon or SAC, or Congress or the public, or even the president. It was an enlivening burden.

And what was their “enlivening burden”? Saving the world:

[My colleagues] shared a feeling—soon transmitted to me—that we were in the most literal sense working to save the world.

What really stood out was this part, where Ellsberg describes how he and his colleagues truly believed the end was nigh:

From the Air Force intelligence estimates I was newly privy to, and the dark view of the Soviets, which my colleagues shared with the whole national security community, I couldn't believe that the world would long escape nuclear holocaust. Alain Enthoven and I were the youngest members of the department. Neither of us joined the extremely generous retirement plan RAND offered. Neither of us believed, in our late twenties, we had a chance of collecting on it.

This reminds me of the report that AI researchers have taken up smoking as a way to signal their belief that AI will cure cancer before smoking kills them.

At this point, I wouldn’t be surprised to hear a lab like Anthropic announce they’re discontinuing all employer-sponsored retirement benefits. It’d be a small sacrifice on behalf of the employees to demonstrate their faith that universal high income is just around the corner. (The corporate cost savings would just be a nice bonus.)

title: Going Somewhere
content:
Life, regardless of location. Chicago, ciao and see you soon.

“Who talks to somebody that they don't know freely, honestly, at six o'clock in the morning?”

The woman driving me home from O'Hare asks it three quarters of the way in. By then the ride has proven her point. She hates airport pickups. “But I do it anyway. I do it, man, for the conversation.”

It is five thirty in the morning and I have fifteen hours of flying behind me. I ordered the Comfort tier because it cost a couple dollars more. You can ask for a quiet ride. The car is newer and it shows up faster. Why not.

My name drops a syllable in America, and I am the one who dropped it. Sim. Like The Sims, like a SIM card. Simone with no photo attached sets up drivers and workers at cafés to expect a lady. Nina Simone here, Simone de Beauvoir there. I'd feel honored with either. She calls me Sim as I open the car's door.

She is a barber who also drives, or a driver who also barbers, depending on the morning. Ten minutes in, she delivers this line: “I'm a recovering addict. Twenty two years. They will never know, because they expect the recovering addict to be looking beat up.”

Back seats stocked: colorful little bags for kids, clothes for whoever can use them. She feeds people most weeks, the ones I often walk past. “I know they name. I will hug them. It could have been me.” She says it as if it's mathematical.

Last Black Friday she and one niece bought another niece a stove and had it delivered. The same girl's father will not buy her a washing machine. “This is your seed you planted, and you're not nurturing it. I don't care how old she is. Everybody needs somebody at some time.” She owns two cars. One sits in a struggling woman's driveway, financed in her name, while the finance company calls her phone. “I'm sidestepping somebody who got it in the car place to give it to somebody who need it.”

When a baby arrives in the family, she says “Welcome to this cruel world. I don't really want to say welcome, but you're here and you gotta thrive. You gotta grow.” She cries at every birth. Six grandchildren so far.

Some mornings her fares are kids headed to school, and she runs the interview. What year are you in. Whatcha gonna do when you get out. Where you plan on being. “This probably some conversation they mama ain't had with them.” Some of them tell her it was the best ride they ever had. She has a reason for asking. “You don't never know who on the edge.”

One night she pulls up to a dark house in some suburb. A kid gets in with his hood up, drawn into the corner of the seat, dressed for disappearing. She turns around before she drives.

“Why are you bagging up in this car? You almost got killed.” He says he is going to football practice. She asks whose name is on the app. His mother's. “You don't have to bag up in the Uber. It's paid for. Your mother called for you.” Then the part he will remember. “You was about to go to hell now. You want to go to the NFL, do it properly. Don't put yourself in danger.”

She read him in one glance. A boy so scared of a stranger's car that he made himself look like the danger. The fear was the costume. She took it off him and drove him to practice.

Then she reads me. “If you don't act scared, they ain't gonna try you.” She glances at my ink and my metal. “You got the piercings. You got that big smile. Ain't nobody gonna just run up on you.” Smiling is public equipment for me. On my own, my face settles to neutral. Elevator, tank top, shades, deep in my own head, and strangers push the button to open the door faster. When I catch it, I send the big smile ahead of me. Walking home at four in the morning in Uptown, I did not catch it. Old fears woke up instead. Big city, late hour, watch yourself, Sim. A woman ahead glanced back at my tank top, the huge blackwork, the piercings, the shades on at night. She picked up her pace. I got as far as “oh, fuck no, I'm the one that people…” and Vicky finished the sentence for me. “You the one that they scared!”

We both burst out laughing.

She has a rule about herself. “If everybody was like me, it'll be a terrible place.” I told her I say that all the fucking time, and I had the receipt. Two weeks earlier a friend bolted mid evening because another friend and I were connecting a bit too much. He read himself as the third wheel. Brother, you're not the third wheel. This is just how we are. If everybody was like us, the world would be a fucking hell. Different lives, same sentences. It kept happening. Neither of us needed anything from the other, so there was nothing to perform.

Vicky was born and raised here. “Been a lot of places, but ain't no place like the Chi.” I have twelve years in, fifteen depending on how you count. I will be tied to this city for the rest of my life. Djo already wrote the song for it, End of Beginning. You take the man out of the city, not the city out the man. Rome stayed in me the whole time here. Chicago is already doing the same in Italy.

“It's a good place. It's a judgmental place. It's a prejudice place.” She's right. Chicago sorts people by map, everybody who lives here knows it. Her car is a shared room. An immigrant from Uptown and a grandmother from the South Side, on God, addiction, stoves, and fear.

Near my street, the money comes up on its own. “This is why I call it the land of milk and honey. I'm out here driving a $53,000 credit to have a conversation with you. At the end of the day this ain't nothing but pennies on the dollar. At the end of the year, Uncle Sam and all the taxes.” I paid thirty two bucks for this ride. “They gave me like sixteen. Half the money. Plus the tip, though. When it comes.”

The app priced the miles and kept half. Everything else in that car was off the books. The Comfort tier sold me a thermostat and the option of silence. The comfort I got was of a different kind. Sixteen dollars, before gas and before Uncle Sam. The tip field asked for a number.

My grazie and my ciao are the signature. Twelve years in this country and I never dropped either one. The accent grants them, and people know they're genuine. She hands back a blessing. I point at the corner and tell her she can stop right here, no need to turn around. But she is already making the turn.

“It don't matter, I'm taking you home. Because I don't know where I'm going after this. But I'm going somewhere.”

Life, regardless of location. Chicago, ciao e a presto.
